extracted.intended_audience: general readers, students, and policy/regulatory practitioners interested in U.S. federal regulatory review
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and standards that govern how the Office of Information and Regulatory Affairs (OIRA) reviews draft federal regulations and guidance (e.g., obligations under Executive Order 12866, the Paperwork Reduction Act, and the Information Quality Act), plus critiques of OIRA's transparency and influence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Review under Executive Order 12866
rubrics_metrics.description: Executive Order 12866 describes OIRA's role in the rulemaking process and directs agencies to follow certain principles, such as consideration of alternatives and analysis of impacts, both benefits and costs. OIRA reviews draft regulations to ensure agency compliance with this executive order.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used as the primary framework for OIRA review of draft rules since 1993; OIRA ensures agencies follow EO12866 principles when developing regulations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of alternatives and impact analysis (benefits and costs)
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies are directed to give 'consideration of alternatives and analysis of impacts, both benefits and costs' when developing rules (principle specified by EO12866).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Regulatory proposals should identify and evaluate reasonable alternatives and provide analysis of expected benefits and costs to support the chosen approach.

rubrics_metrics.name: Focus on 'economically significant' rules
rubrics_metrics.description: The executive order states OIRA should focus on 'economically significant' rules. Of the 500 to 700 rules reviewed by OIRA annually, about 100 have been classified as 'economically significant'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OIRA prioritizes review resources on rules that meet the 'economically significant' classification (per EO12866 guidance).

rubrics_metrics.name: Paperwork Reduction Act compliance and oversight
rubrics_metrics.description: The Paperwork Reduction Act (1980, updated 1995) established OIRA in OMB and governs OIRA's role in reviewing information collection burdens and related processes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agencies must comply with the Paperwork Reduction Act's requirements for information collection and justification; OIRA reviews and enforces those obligations as part of its remit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Information Quality Act oversight
rubrics_metrics.description: OIRA oversees the implementation of government-wide policies in information quality and reviews draft regulations under the Information Quality Act.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agencies are expected to follow Information Quality Guidelines; OIRA coordinates and enforces quality standards for information used in rules and guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Application of Circular A-4 and Good Guidance Practices
rubrics_metrics.description: OIRA guides and coordinates agencies with respect to Circular A-4, Information Quality Guidelines, and the Bulletin for Agency Good Guidance Practices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agencies should follow Circular A-4 methodological guidance for regulatory analysis and adhere to the Bulletin for Good Guidance Practices when developing non-rule guidance; OIRA coordinates these expectations across agencies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Review of guidance documents and interagency conflict resolution (EO13422)
rubrics_metrics.description: Executive Order 13422 (2007) changed rules to include federal agencies' 'guidance documents' in OIRA review and specified procedures for the resolution of conflicts between or among agencies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Under EO13422 (as described on the page), OIRA's review scope extended beyond regulations to guidance documents and set processes for resolving interagency disagreements; this expansion was controversial in Congress.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope of OIRA review across policy areas
rubrics_metrics.description: OIRA develops and oversees implementation of government-wide policies in areas including information technology, information policy, privacy, and statistical policy; it reviews draft rules received from federal agencies under multiple laws.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OIRA's review standards apply across these subject-matter branches (Food/Health/Labor; Information Policy; Natural Resources/Environment; Statistical & Science Policy; Transportation & Security), implying subject-specific expertise and considerations during review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transparency and public disclosure of proposed changes and evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Criticism: OIRA 'routinely declines to release the changes it has proposed, the evidence it has relied upon to make them, or the identities and affiliations of White House advisers and other agencies' staff it has consulted' and 'conducts much of its business in secret' and is 'exempt from most Freedom of Information Act requests.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: As an evaluative standard, transparency about edits, evidence, and consulted parties is highlighted as a concern; a transparent review process would disclose proposed changes, supporting evidence, and participants.

rubrics_metrics.name: Safeguards against undue influence by regulated parties
rubrics_metrics.description: Criticism/metric: a 2003 GAO report stated that 'regulated parties,' typically corporations or their lobbyists, frequently get what they want after meetings with OIRA.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluation of OIRA's process should consider whether appropriate safeguards exist to prevent disproportionate influence by regulated interests (e.g., disclosure of meetings, equal access policies).

rubrics_metrics.name: Extent to which OIRA alters agency submissions
rubrics_metrics.description: Reported metric: a 2011 report from the Center on Progressive Reform stated that in 10 years, OIRA altered 84 percent of EPA rule submissions (as well as 65 percent of proposed rules from other agencies).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The frequency and magnitude of post-submission alterations by OIRA function as an indicator of OIRA's influence and are relevant when assessing the balance between centralized review and agency expertise/autonomy.
